record.original_question: How can hundreds of phytoplankton species coexist while competing for only one or a few limiting nutrients, even though the principle of competitive exclusion predicts that at equilibrium only one or a few species should remain? Can a nonequilibrium model that combines turbulent water advection, species-specific drift relative to the water, regeneration of the limiting nutrient, and species-dependent nutrient uptake and growth explain sustained coexistence of many plankton species?

evidence.quote: According to the principle of competitive exclusion, the final equilibrium state should be taken over by one or a few species according to the limiting factors. On the other hand, in reality hundreds species of the plankton coexist. This paradoxical question was first raised by Hutchinson [7].

We believe that the essential mechanism of the plankton drifting can be captured by such a modeling. Let f(t, x) be the density of the limiting resource (deficient neutrient), and ρn(t, x) be the densities of different species of plankton, n = 1, 2, · · · , N.

artifact.status_search_result: The paradox of the plankton, posed by Hutchinson (1961), has been addressed by many partial mechanistic resolutions: chaotic/turbulent mixing along fractal sets, mesoscale vortex transport barriers, oscillations and chaos in resource competition models, size-selective grazing, environmental fluctuations, and spatial heterogeneity have all been shown to permit coexistence of more species than limiting resources in specific models. No single universally accepted mechanism explains observed plankton diversity, and the question of whether nonequilibrium advection–reaction–diffusion models of the stated form can rigorously support coexistence of arbitrarily many species under realistic assumptions remains an active research topic. Hence the problem is best characterized as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Paradox of the plankton - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The paradox can be resolved by factors such as: chaotic fluid motion; size-selective grazing; spatio-temporal heterogeneity; or environmental fluctuations.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple partial mechanisms have been proposed but no single resolution is universally accepted.

status_evidence.title: Mesoscale vortices and the paradox of the plankton
status_evidence.snippet: Ocean mesoscale vortices generate transport barriers and incomplete horizontal mixing, allowing for a prolonged survival of the less-fit species.
status_evidence.claim: Advective transport barriers can sustain coexistence of competing plankton species in models.

status_evidence.title: A model for resolving the plankton paradox: coexistence in open flows
status_evidence.snippet: Strong chaotic mixing along a fractal set and the boundary layer around the obstacle are responsible for the coexistence.
status_evidence.claim: Chaotic advection in open flows is a known partial resolution for the plankton paradox.
